Tristan klipfish (Bovichtus diacanthus) is a benthic notothenioid endemic to the cold, well-oxygenated waters surrounding the Tristan da Cunha archipelago. The onset of exogenous feeding in this species is preceded by a relatively brief developmental period within the yolk-sac larva stage. At a mean water temperature of 12.6 °C [T = 12.6 °C], the age at which free-swimming larvae begin exogenous feeding occurs at approximately 34 days [ab = approximately 34 days]. The newly emerged prolarvae are minute, possessing a wet weight at birth of just 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a value consistent with the small egg diameter of 1.5 millimeters that characterizes this species. This extremely low initial mass reflects the lecithotrophic strategy of the endotrophic larva, which relies entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before the mouth opens and active prey capture begins. The energetic constraints imposed by such a small body size at the start of the pelagic larval phase likely influence subsequent growth trajectories and survivorship in the planktonic environment.

Growth in the pelagic larval phase proceeds rapidly under favorable thermal conditions. Early larval development is characterized by the progressive resorption of the yolk sac and the differentiation of key feeding structures, including the jaw apparatus and the digestive tract. Throughout the juvenile and early adult stages, individuals continue to accumulate biomass, gradually approaching the asymptotic body dimensions typical of the species. The ultimate total length attained by Tristan klipfish has been documented at 18.9 centimeters [Li = 18.9 centimeters], representing the maximum size recorded for this species in the wild. This asymptotic length is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 86.8 grams [Wwi = 86.8 grams], a value that describes the heaviest adults encountered in the population. The progression from the pubertal size of 12 centimeters to the ultimate length of 18.9 centimeters represents a sustained period of growth that likely spans several years. The length-weight relationship in this species suggests a positively allometric growth pattern, where increases in length are accompanied by a disproportionately greater increase in mass, a common phenomenon in marine fishes that occupy benthic habitats.
